title: How Barbie Doll Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the Barbie doll, from Ruth and Elliott Handler's founding of Mattel and the 1959 debut, through Barbie's friends and family, the Ken and Barbie relationship, Barbie's many careers, and feminist critiques. They cover Mattel's missteps on race (Colored Francie, Black Barbie, the Oreo Barbie controversy), body image concerns and the Barbie figure's real-world proportions, Teen Talk Barbie and the Barbie Liberation Organization, and Mattel's aggressive trademark enforcement against artists and parodists (Aqua's "Barbie Girl," Paul David, Barbara Bell). The episode also includes a segment with Gordon Mulvena... (see note) founder of the Bathroom Reader Institute about Uncle John's Bathroom Reader, and a closing run-through of unusual Barbie releases.

segments.title: Science Channel TV show announcement and intro
segments.summary: Hosts promote their upcoming Science Channel TV show premiere and iTunes availability, then open the episode and discuss Uncle John's Bathroom Reader and the Barbie episode's sponsorship-like tie-in.
topics: Stuff You Should Know TV show

segments.title: Shout-out to horror fiction contest entrant
segments.summary: Hosts give a shout-out to Jay McMurray, whose self-published story The Mind Reader is on Amazon.

segments.title: Ruth and Elliott Handler and the founding of Mattel
segments.summary: Ruth Marianna (later Ruth Handler) grows up poor in Denver; she meets Elliott Handler, and they move to California. Elliott makes picture frames and Ruth handles marketing; together with Harold Matson they found Mattel. They have children Barbie and Ken.

segments.title: Barbie's inspiration and the Lilli doll
segments.summary: Barbie was inspired by Ruth's daughter playing with adult paper dolls. Mattel's male executives initially rejected a three-dimensional fashion doll. Ruth found the German Lilli doll on a trip to Switzerland. Mattel agreed to make Barbie, who debuted at the 1959 Toy Fair in New York with a zebra-stripe swimsuit and sideways-glancing eyes. Sears initially balked, but the doll sold well in the first year.

segments.title: Sideways-glancing doll eyes and Shinto doll burning
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why painted doll eyes looking to the side never meet the viewer's gaze, and mention Shinto beliefs about dolls capturing spirits, with an annual doll-burning ceremony at Meiji Shrine.

segments.title: Ruth Handler's later life and Nearly Me
segments.summary: Ruth Handler developed breast cancer and, unable to find a satisfactory prosthesis, founded Nearly Me, which made prostheses for cancer survivors. She died of cancer. The Handlers were forced out of Mattel after questionable earnings reports in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Elliott died the previous year at age nineties.

segments.title: Barbie sales stats and Barbie's fictional biography
segments.summary: The hosts cite sales figures (a Barbie sells about every three seconds, a $1.5 billion business, girls aged three to six own about twelve). The best-selling Barbie is Totally Hair Barbie. Barbie's full name is given as Barbara Millicent Roberts, from Willows, Wisconsin; Ken was introduced in 1961; Midge, Skipper, Stacy, Todd and Chelsea are family and friends.

segments.title: Midge pregnancy controversy and Ken's history
segments.summary: Midge was introduced pregnant, causing controversy in two releases, the second around 2002 or 2006. Ken's Malibu and Magic Earring Ken line, introduced in 1993 and embraced by the gay community, was pulled from shelves after Mattel was surprised by the reaction. Barbie and Ken broke up in 2004 and reunited on Valentine's Day 2011.

segments.title: Barbie's careers and pets
segments.summary: The hosts list Barbie's many careers (fashion model, astronaut, paleontologist, police officer, drive-through and franchise jobs, race car driver, aerobics instructor) and her band Barbie and the Rockers, plus her more than fifty pets.

segments.title: Feminist critiques of Barbie
segments.summary: Barbie and second-wave feminism developed together in the early 1960s (Barbie in 1959, Friedan's The Feminine Mystique in 1963). Critics object to her figure, wealth, and materialism. Mattel defends Barbie as a career woman who has held many jobs and is never married. A 2010 Washington and Lee study found girls shown a Barbie in a male-dominated job reported they could do the same.

segments.title: Teen Talk Barbie and the Barbie Liberation Organization
segments.summary: Teen Talk Barbie spoke four random phrases from 270, including 'Math class is tough,' which drew criticism from the American Association of University Women; Mattel offered replacements. The Barbie Liberation Organization swapped voice chips between Teen Talk Barbies and talking G.I. Joes. The Simpsons episode 'Lisa vs. Malibu Stacy' is noted.

segments.title: Race and diversity missteps
segments.summary: Mattel's missteps include Colored Francie (1967 in the hosts' account, 'ninety seven' in the transcript), Black Barbie (1980s), African American Ken, and Oreo-themed Barbie whose Black version said 'Oreo' and was pulled. Mattel's international dolls use stereotyped costumes, such as a Mexican Ken in a sombrero. African American Barbies Kara, Grace, and Teresa were introduced later with more realistic features.

segments.title: Barbie body image and real-life proportions
segments.summary: Barbie's figure was reportedly designed by women to fit miniature fashion clothes. Studies found girls who played with Barbie had poorer body image; a 2011 Dutch study found average-sized dolls led to more snacking. Life-size Barbie proportions are compared to real-world measures, and Cindy Jackson and Valeria Lukyanova are discussed as people who resemble Barbie.
